we have isolated and characterized a novel transporter for antimicrobial peptides, the SapABCDF system, in Salmonella.

(i) we have isolated genes from S. typhimururium which are necessary for resistance to antimicrobials and are involved in virulence, (ii) these genes are part of an operon, and (iii) the SapABCDF system appears to be a novel transporter for peptides.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the molecular basis of bacterial resistance to host antimicrobial peptides and its relationship to the mechanisms of virulence.
the identification, cloning, and characterization of the genes required for the resistance to antimicrobial cationic peptides in Salmonella.
the molecular genetic analysis of a novel locus required for resistance of Salmonella typhymurium to antimicrobial peptides.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the sap operon encodes a novel ABC transporter that mediates resistance to cationic antimicrobial peptides in bacteria.
the SapABCDF system is a novel transporter for antimicrobial peptides.
the SapABCDF system represents the first identified bacterial system for peptide transport that has a role in virulency.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
SapABCDF is a novel transporter for antimicrobial peptides and the first one with a periplasmatic component involved in virulence.
the sap system is involved in the uptake and utilization of peptides and in resistance to antimicrobial agents.
the sap genes encode a periplasm‐localized ABC‐type peptide transporter, which is essential for resistance to the antimicrobials protamine and melittin and is involved in virulence.
The main takeaway from our work is that

the SapABCDF system, which is required for resistance to the antimicrobials melittin and cecropin P1 and is essential for virulence in mice, is the first identified transporter for antimicrobial peptides.
the Sap transporter system is required for the virulence of S. typhimururium and for resistance to antimicrobials such as the peptide melittin and the cationic polypeptide protamine.
Salmonella has evolved a mechanism to protect itself from host defense peptides, a strategy which has been coopted by many pathogens to facilitate infection.
